title: NFT ownership disputes - how Indian courts might approach them
p1: You bought an NFT. You own the digital asset, right? Not always. The biggest confusion around NFTs is that owning a token may not mean owning every legal right connected to it.
p2: Many people assume an NFT purchase works like buying a physical painting. But an NFT is usually a digital certificate recorded on a blockchain, while copyright, commercial rights, and usage permissions may remain with someone else. This difference could become a major issue when Indian courts examine NFT ownership disputes.
p3: Indian courts may look beyond the blockchain record and examine contracts, promises made during the sale, intellectual property rights, and the actual intention of the parties. A blockchain entry can show who holds a token, but the law may still need to decide what that ownership legally includes. The practical lesson: before buying or creating NFTs, check the rights attached to them, not just the token itself.
conclusion: Do you think blockchain records should be enough to prove ownership in Indian courts, or should traditional legal rights come first?
